title: europe bets big electrification now it needs people plug 2026 07 21
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, July 21 (Reuters) - Europe has one answer for almost every major energy challenge it faces: electrify.
Want to cut emissions? Electrify. Want to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels? Electrify. Want to shield consumers from volatile gas markets? Electrify. Want to restore energy security after Russia's invasion of Ukraine? Electrify.
The strategy is logical. As Europe fills ​its power system with wind, solar, hydro and nuclear generation, replacing fossil-fuel consumption with electricity should lower emissions, improve efficiency and shrink the region's energy-import bill.
The European Commission has now gone so ‌far as to set out a vision of making Europe the world's first "electro-powered" continent, targeting a sharp increase in electricity's share of final energy consumption.
But Europe's energy transition is entering a more difficult phase. Building renewable power generation was the relatively easy part. Convincing millions of households, drivers and industrial firms to use more electricity may prove far harder.
The challenge facing policymakers is that electrification is no longer primarily an engineering problem. It is becoming an economic one.
For years, Europe's energy debate focused on supply. Governments raced to install wind ​turbines and solar panels, strengthen grids and reduce reliance on Russian gas.
That effort has produced meaningful results. Renewables now account for nearly half of EU electricity generation, according to the European Commission.
Now attention is shifting ​toward demand.
The Commission estimates electricity accounts for only around 23% of final energy consumption today, despite years of progress in clean power generation.
To meet the bloc's climate and ⁠competitiveness goals, that share needs to rise substantially, and fast.
That means persuading drivers to buy electric vehicles, homeowners to install heat pumps and factories to replace fossil-fuel processes with electric alternatives.
In theory, this should be happening already.
Electric motors are ​vastly more efficient than combustion engines. Heat pumps can deliver several units of heat for every unit of electricity consumed. Electrified industrial processes can reduce emissions while improving energy efficiency.
Electrification is also a cornerstone of two of Europe's key ​concerns — energy security and competitiveness — because it reduces dependence on imported fuels, as the International Energy Agency has recently noted.
The problem is that consumers and companies respond to economics, not theory.
Europe wants people to use more electricity, yet it remains significantly more expensive than fossil fuels. The Commission itself acknowledges that power prices can still be roughly three times the cost of gas — a major obstacle to wider adoption.
That contradiction sits at the heart of Europe's electrification conundrum.
A household considering whether to replace a functioning gas boiler with a heat pump ​may support decarbonization in principle.
But if the upfront costs are high, due to financing costs and elevated electricity prices, many will postpone the decision.
The same applies to industry.
European manufacturers are already grappling with concerns about competitiveness relative to rivals ​in the United States and China. Asking those companies to electrify operations becomes much harder if doing so raises production costs in the near term.
The warning signs are already beginning to appear.
Heat pumps were once one of the fastest-growing segments of Europe's ‌energy transition. After ⁠years of rapid expansion, sales slowed sharply in 2023 as gas prices fell, interest rates rose and policy support became less certain.
The European Commission's Joint Research Centre reported a decline in sales after the record growth seen in 2022, while industry groups have warned of investment delays and job losses.
That slowdown matters because heat pumps represent one of the clearest and most cost-effective pathways for electrifying buildings.
More broadly, Europe's experience highlights a reality that policymakers sometimes underestimate: consumers do not adopt energy technologies simply because they are cleaner. They adopt them when they are affordable, convenient and reliable.
The continent faces another obstacle as well.
Electrification requires an enormous expansion of networks. New wind farms and solar projects are of limited ​value if grids cannot connect them. Electric vehicles require ​charging infrastructure. Factories need power connections. Homes need upgraded ⁠distribution networks.
Yet grid bottlenecks have become commonplace across much of Europe, with connection queues stretching for years in some markets. The Commission has repeatedly identified slow grid development as a major barrier to electrification.
None of this means Europe's strategy is wrong.
In fact, the long-term logic remains compelling. The bloc imports large quantities of fossil fuels and spent roughly 380 billion ​euros ($434 billion) on fuel imports in 2024, according to the IEA.
Reducing that dependence would strengthen both energy security and economic resilience.
The question is whether policymakers have adequately accounted ​for the gap between the desired ⁠destination and the path required to reach it.
Europe has spent much of the past decade focused on how to generate clean electricity. The next decade will be defined by a different challenge: how to make electricity the obvious economic choice.
That means lower power prices, faster grid construction, stable incentives and fewer barriers to investment. Without those reforms, electrification risks becoming the bottleneck in Europe's energy transition rather than its engine.
The continent's clean-energy future ultimately depends on something surprisingly simple. Europeans do not merely ⁠need abundant clean ​electricity.
They need a compelling reason to use it.
